div.head: Chapter 27
div.p: And because "the right of the king or prince and the right of the subjects or of the whole community are judged to be equal. And this doctrine is given by a clear text in c. 1, § ex eadem, De lege Corradi, which the Doctors collect in c. i, de forma fidelitatis, et in c. de forma, 22, q. 5, where it is held that the lord is bound and obligated by the same fidelity to his subject or vassal as the vassal is to the lord" and there are many laws pertaining to this: from this it follows that the king, prince, or lord is obliged, as the political head, to defend and free the whole body and kingdom from hardships, harms, and necessities, as the natural head, insofar as it can, provides for itself and occupies itself with governance to acquire the good and resist the evil that may come to all the other members.

From this it follows that the king is bound — in order to free his subjects if they suffer any servitude or pressure and wrongs that they cannot bear from adversaries — to wage war and to die in it if necessary, in order to liberate them, especially against tyrants who hold his subjects by force. For one reason, on account of his own interest, for injury is done to him and harm caused to him by not having his vassals or subjects free to be able to dispose of them without impediment in whatever is fitting for himself and the kingdom. Whence it is lawful for him to aid oppressed subjects: ff., quod metus causa, L. etsi in partes, § 1, "for I am able to free my vassals and men from your tyranny with an armed hand. Each person makes use of his natural right and also his civil right": L. si servas, Codex, De his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt. For another reason, to avoid the injuries and harms to the kingdom, and because the violence of the tyrant is always permanent and in continuous and enduring act — not in a passing act —, by which it not only continually inflicts violence on the very subjects, making them obey out of fear, but also on the kings or lords: on those, that is the subjects, compulsive violence; on these, that is the kings or lords, expulsive violence, as is noted in C. de vi et vi armata, L. 1, § penult., in glosa. For this reason, the right to wage war against the tyrant is also acquired by the lords on account of the expulsive violence, whenever and as often as they have the opportunity. For if the prince has been expelled from his principality or dominion, he can recover it by his own authority as often as the occasion presents itself, and it will be said that he has recovered it in the act: Jason, in L. clam possidere, § qui ad nundinas, ff., De adquirenda possessione. And likewise to the subjects is acquired the right to declare war against the tyrant on account of the compulsive violence, and to kill him, because it is lawful for everyone to redeem their own blood: ff., De bonis eorum, L. 1a. and to defend their liberty: ff., De captivis et postliminiis, L. nihil interest. And above all because the tyrant is said to be the murderer of as many persons as he reduces to servitude: ut 22, q. 4, § sed et cum his, et est capitulo sub can. inter cetera et ibi glossa. And a continuing personal injury is inflicted on a living man for as long as his liberty is taken from him, or he is held in servitude, or any other harm is unjustly suffered in his person; from which violence is committed each day and the right to resist it arises each day. Therefore it can be resisted each day. And such liberation has the character of a recovery made in the act, even if the opportunity to liberate oneself had not presented itself until a thousand years later: Baldo, in L. vis ezus, Codex, De probationibus. Whence not only one people, one kingdom or province, but also any particular oppressed person has just war against the tyrant who oppresses them and can kill him. Where Baldo says that if a man is detained by force for a very long time: since violence is committed each day, it can be resisted each day. The same is said in ff. De usufructu acrescendo, L. 1, in fin. Thus Baldo.

And Lucas de Pena in L. prohibitum, Codex, De jure fiscis, Lib. 10, says that when it is notorious that a captive is being held against justice, it is lawful for him to kill those who detain him, if he cannot otherwise secure his safety: let him secure it however he can. He cites L. nihil interest, ff. De captivis et postliminus and notes 1 Dist., c. ius gentium; ad idem 50 Dist., quod vero; Digest., ex quibus causis maiores, L. succurritur; pertinent is Digest., De edicto, ff., L. bovem, § si servus. Indeed, capital punishment is incurred by one who, having been unjustly captured, does not flee when he is able: ff., De re militari, L. non omnes, qui captus. For it is imputed as fault to one who is able to return and does not.

The tyrant can therefore justly be killed not only by the king or lord, or by the whole community that he unjustly holds or oppresses, but also by any member of the people. This is to be understood of the tyrant who usurps another's kingdom, so as to preserve the declaration or decree of the Council of Constance, Session 1, 16; Saint Thomas, Sentences, dist. 44 q. 2 a. 2 ad 5 et lib. 1, cap. 6, De regimine principum; 2.2 q. 64 a. 3, and this in any manner and in any way whatsoever: laying ambushes and making use of opportunities by night or by day, or in whatever opportunity presents the occasion for doing it, or whenever one finds the convenience. The reason is that all things of this kind are lawful for one who has continuous just war, unless a greater danger of tyranny for the multitude is feared to follow from such an occasion: Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 42 a. 2 ad 3, unless faith that was pledged is thereby broken, which must be kept even toward an enemy, as we have already said.

Since, then, the peoples of Peru, the children and heirs of King Atahualpa and all the peoples of that kingdom and those kingdoms, now see and have seen their king seized unjustly and tyrannically and afterwards killed, and many other peoples likewise, and all those kingdoms placed in servitude, their liberty lost, their states and dignities usurped, their jurisdictions and royal rights possessed by tyrants, their immense treasures robbed; and that through the repartimientos, the peoples and the natural lords who are heirs of the said King Atahualpa and other lords, and all private persons, live in continual and harsh oppression, and see themselves every hour — from the time the Spaniards entered those lands — diminishing and coming to an end: it is manifest, and will be manifest even to any barbarians, that from the moment they entered there and carried out the deeds of which we treat, the right was acquired by the peoples and by the whole kingdom and kingdoms to make war upon the Spaniards. For one purpose, to free their king while he lived; for another, after his death, to restore his heirs to those states and kingdoms he held, and those which might belong to them after the death of the king of Cuzco called Huáscar, his brother; for another, to restore the many other lords they have despoiled, and all of them in their dignities and royal rights; for another, to liberate all those kingdoms from the hands of the tyrants and to recover their pristine liberty; for another, to recover the innumerable treasures they robbed; for another, so that each private person may redeem themselves from the vexation and tyrannical servitude in which every hour they see themselves and their lineage perishing.

Likewise the royal heirs of Atahualpa and the other lords have the same right on account of their own interest and to aid the peoples and free them from so great adversity, harms, and irreparable evils: they have acquired and have the most powerful right of natural law to wage war against the Spaniards as their proper and true tyrants. Not only the kings and the peoples and the kingdom in common, but each private person has the same right given them by natural law. So that not only the lords — summoning peoples, assembling armies, and waging public war — and the peoples themselves uniting to wage it can most justly kill and annihilate the Spaniards without leaving any memory of them; but any Indian in particular can do so most justly by the same authority, asleep or awake, from behind or from before, or in whatever manner the opportunity presents itself, as has been proved. And the general reason why any member of the people or community or kingdom can kill the said tyrants in the said ways is that they are already challenged by the whole republic, tacitly or expressly. As regards the express or public challenge — that is, by name — it appears in the case of the Outlaw. As regards the tacit challenge, that is, the one who is truly an enemy of the city, of the kingdom, and of the fatherland, who by force or oppression has seized or usurped the principality over a free people, against the will of the citizens or having forced them to consent, taking away their entire liberty — and yet on account of his power no one dares to aspire to the liberation of the commonwealth —: while his tyranny endures, the people or kingdom seems to have tacitly challenged him and to have regarded him as a public enemy, and consequently the power to lawfully kill him is understood to be given to any member of the people. Whence Saint Thomas, 2 Sentences, dist. 44, a. penult., ad ultimum, says that "when there is no recourse to a superior, it is praiseworthy that the tyrant — who by violence and fear made himself lord over unwilling subjects or those forced to consent — should be killed by a private person." Thus from him. Add to the same the same Saint Thomas: "unless a greater harm to the kingdom or multitude would follow from it than from the very rule of the tyrant itself": 2.2 q. 42 a. 2 ad 3; et lib. 1, cap. 6, De regimine principum. It remains then manifest that the peoples of those kingdoms and lands of Peru have just war against the Spaniards, for the purpose of recovering as much as possible of the injustices received and obtaining satisfaction for so great evils and harms.
